        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis.

        3. add all changed file to git changes

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the whole workflow.  
Everything is written for a Unix‑like shell (Linux/macOS). If you’re on Windows, use PowerShell or WSL.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you don’t have SSH keys set up, use the HTTPS URL instead:
> `git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Detect the predominant language

> In a typical Node.js project the majority of the code will be in `.js` or `.ts`.  
> We’ll assume **JavaScript** (or TypeScript) is the dominant language.

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content:

```dockerfile
# 2.2 Dockerfile – Node.js + Alpine
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Build (if you have a build step – otherwise skip)
# RUN npm run build

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:20-alpine` is lightweight and contains the latest LTS Node.js.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install.  
> * The app is assumed to listen on port **3000** – adjust if your app uses a different port.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory `k8s` and add `deployment.yaml` inside it:

```yaml
# 2.3 k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change if you use another registry
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80          # Service port
      targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **Notes**  
> * Adjust `image:` to point to the registry you’ll push to (GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, etc.).  
> * `replicas: 2` gives you a minimal HA setup – tweak as needed.  
> * The service is `ClusterIP`; change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# 2.4 .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  pull_request:

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          echo ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} | docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} --password-stdin
          docker push ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Tag latest
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        run: |
          docker tag ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
          docker push ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What this workflow does**  
> 1. Checks out the repo.  
> 2. Installs Node.js 20 and caches `npm`.  
> 3. Runs `npm ci` and `npm test`.  
> 4. Builds a Docker image, pushes it to GitHub Container Registry (GCR).  
> 5. On pushes to `main`, tags the image as `latest`.

> **Prerequisites**  
> * The repo must have a `Dockerfile` (we just created one).  
> * The repo must have a `package.json` with a test script (`npm test`).  
> * The GitHub Actions runner needs Docker (the default `ubuntu-latest` image has it).  
> * The `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret is automatically available; it has permission to push to GCR.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
# 3. Add all new/changed files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you want to see what’s staged:

```bash
git status
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
# 4. Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 4. Push to remote
git push origin main
```

> After the push, GitHub Actions will automatically trigger the workflow you just added.  
> You can view the build status in the **Actions** tab of the repository.

---

### Quick sanity check

1. **Verify Dockerfile** – run locally:

   ```bash
   docker build -t test-nodejs-welcome .
   docker run -p 3000:3000 test-nodejs-welcome
   ```

   Open `http://localhost:3000` to confirm the app is reachable.

2. **Verify Kubernetes manifests** – apply them to a cluster:

   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
   kubectl get all
   ```

   You should see a deployment, pods, and a service.

---

## 🎉 Done!

You now have:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys the app to Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes Docker images |

Feel free to tweak the image name, registry, or Kubernetes settings to match your environment. Happy coding!
